extracted.subtask_description: Writing or editing newspaper articles reporting wartime events, combining official statements, eyewitness accounts, operational details, political reactions, and legal context for a general readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute to official sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite and attribute factual material to authoritative government sources (War Department, White House, State Department) when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly cites the War Department, the President's statement, and the State Department note as sources. Example: 'The War Department’s detailed description of the American bombing of Tokio disclosed...' and 'The President’s statement ... was received from him at Corpus Christi, Tex., along with a note of protest from the State Department.' Use official attributions for claims about operations, casualties, and diplomatic communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish full texts of official communications when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the full text or extended excerpts of important official statements or diplomatic notes in the body of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This page reproduces 'The President’s Statement' and the 'State Department’s Note' (TEXT OF THE UNITED STATES REPLY...), providing verbatim wording for readers. When an official communication is central to the story (e.g., a diplomatic protest or presidential statement), publishing the text supports transparency and allows readers to judge tone and content directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify individuals by name and hometown
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting casualties, prisoners, or participants, provide full names and home addresses or hometowns where available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists the names and hometowns/addresses of the flyers ('Second ... Farrow of Washington, D. C.; First Lieut. Robert L. Hite of ...'). Use this level of identification for military personnel involved in notable events, while observing security/privacy considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish confirmed vs. unconfirmed information
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly label reports that are 'confirmed', 'reported', 'presumed', or 'unconfirmed' and provide dates of confirmation where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text differentiates: 'It was not until March 12, 1943, that the American Government received the communication ... stating that these Americans had in fact been tried...' and uses terms like 'prisoners or presumed to be prisoners.' Maintain such qualifiers when sources are incomplete or evolving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect operational security; withhold sensitive details when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and report when information was withheld for security reasons and explain the rationale for such secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The War Department withheld full details 'as long as possible' to protect the flyers and operations; the article explains the secrecy: 'The preoccupation in bringing American flyers to safety was a principal reason why no detailed statement was issued.' Reporters should note when and why details were omitted to avoid endangering personnel or operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide background and historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply the operational history and background necessary to understand the current event (origins, training, platforms, timeline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives detailed background on the Doolittle raid (planning in January 1942, training, the Hornet as base, changes in plan after being sighted). Use timelines, origins of plans, and prior events to situate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include eyewitness and participant accounts for human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate first-person recollections and anecdotes from participants to add human detail and immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: interviews with Doolittle's flyers describing takeoff, bailout, hardships, and humor ('We stuffed these things into the others’ pockets...'). Use such accounts to humanize the story, while corroborating factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain legal and international-law context where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting alleged violations (e.g., treatment of prisoners), cite relevant legal instruments and specific articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State Department note references the Geneva Prisoners of War Convention and cites Articles I, LX, LXI, LXII, LXV, LXVI with specific procedural protections. When reporting alleged war crimes or POW treatment, include the relevant treaty provisions and explain their implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report a range of official and political reactions with attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and present reactions from government officials, legislators, and military leaders, attributing each statement to its speaker and office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece quotes Speaker Sam Rayburn, House Minority Leader Joseph W. Martin Jr., Senators, and Representative statements. Present diverse political responses and identify speakers and roles to show the spectrum of official reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present policy debate and cautions (avoid simple advocacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include voices urging restraint or caution along with those calling for reprisals to reflect policy debate and context for potential actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article prints both calls for vengeance and warnings against retaliation in kind ('We must not retaliate in kind because ... we must not make unwise strategic decisions based on our anger.'). Balance emotive calls with strategic/policy cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide operational and technical specifics when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Give concrete tactical details (altitudes, armament, targets, routes) to inform readers about how the operation was conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: bombers climbed to 1,500 feet for bombing, used 500-pound demolition bombs and four-pound incendiaries, employed a 20-cent sight. Such specifics improve readers' understanding but should be weighed against security and sensitivity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain reasons for key decisions and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the operational or strategic reasons behind important decisions (e.g., plan changes, timing) and link them to outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains Doolittle's decision to change plans after the task force was sighted and how that forced longer flights and subsequent crash-landings. Explaining cause-and-effect helps readers understand constraints and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear datelines and dates for statements and events
rubrics_metrics.description: Date events and official communications precisely (datelines like 'WASHINGTON, April 21' and explicit dates for notes/statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This article uses datelines and dates for the President's statement and the State Department reply ('Apri, 12, 1943'). Precise dating aids reader comprehension and historical record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify casualties and damage with specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide numbers and concrete descriptions for casualties, prisoners, interned persons, and material damage when verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text quantifies: 'of the eighty officers and men on the flight, one was killed, two are missing, eight are prisoners or presumed to be prisoners of Japan, five are interned in Russia and sixty-four ... got home through China.' Similarly, list factory/plant damage specifics when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations for emphasis and authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Include verbatim quotes from principals (president, generals, participants) to convey tone and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reproduces direct words: Roosevelt: 'This recourse by our enemies to frightfulness is barbarous,' General Arnold: 'We must not rest—we must redouble our efforts...' Use quotes to convey official tone and emotional force, and attribute them precisely.
